claims.text: Resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings is primarily governed by multilayer-interface coherency.
Coherent multilayer interfaces generate localized back-stresses.
Incoherent interfaces lack the well-defined stress fields attributed to coherent interfaces.
The absence of well-defined interface stress fields facilitates dislocation motion and accelerates time-dependent deformation.
Minor Al additions to alternating CoCrFeMnNi-based layers can control lattice-parameter mismatch and interface coherency.
Controlled Al addition can deliberately produce an incoherent-interface coating series.
Testing at 0.4–0.6 Tm accelerates creep phenomena in the proposed coatings.
Coatings with coherent interfaces will have lower steady-state creep rates than coatings with incoherent interfaces under identical test conditions.
Coatings with coherent interfaces will show a delayed onset of plastic deformation relative to coatings with incoherent interfaces.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to CoCrFeMnNi-based high-entropy alloys at 0.4–0.6 Tm under accelerated-creep conditions.
If the coherent- and incoherent-interface series exhibit no statistically significant difference in creep rate or deformation onset, interface coherency is not the controlling factor.
If local chemistry, rather than interface coherency, correlates with mechanical behavior, the proposed primary-coherency mechanism is falsified.

contradictions.description: The baseline says the two series differ only in interface coherency, but the intervention produces incoherency through Al addition, which necessarily changes local chemistry; the uncertainty field acknowledges this compositional confound.
